title: Two Kinds of Devotion
script: Bayu: [thoughtful] You visit Ibu every Friday like clockwork, and yet somehow I'm the one who ends up handling every actual crisis at two in the morning.
Salma: Visibility isn't the same as absence, Bayu. I coordinate her medication, her appointments, half of it invisibly, from a distance you never seem to notice.
Bayu: [carefully] Invisible to me, perhaps, but remarkably visible to everyone else, given how often it surfaces in conversation at family gatherings.
Salma: Are you suggesting I mention it deliberately, as though caring for our mother were some kind of reputation management exercise?
Bayu: [reflective] I'm suggesting the mentioning happens often enough that I've started wondering which of us is caring for her, and which of us is curating an image of caring for her.
Salma: That's a cruel thing to say, even if some sliver of it might be uncomfortably accurate.
Bayu: [honestly] I don't say it to wound you. I say it because I've caught myself doing the opposite lately, resenting the invisibility of my own effort rather than simply offering it.
Salma: You, resentful of being unseen? I assumed you preferred it that way, given how rarely you mention any of it yourself.
Bayu: [gently] I preferred it in principle. In practice, some tired, petty part of me wants credit too, which unsettles me more than admitting the exhaustion ever did.
Salma: So neither of us is quite as untainted by the desire for recognition as we'd like the other to believe.
Bayu: [calmly] Apparently not. Perhaps the real question isn't who's more devoted, but whether either of us can keep showing up once the audience, real or imagined, disappears entirely.
Salma: I'd like to think I would. I'm less certain than I was five minutes ago, which is probably the most honest thing either of us has said tonight.
Bayu: [encouraging] Then let's agree on something smaller than certainty. No more mentioning it at gatherings, from either of us, starting this weekend.
Salma: Agreed. And Bayu, call me at two in the morning next time. I'd rather share the invisible part too.

quiz.question: What is Bayu's initial complaint against Salma?
options: She spends too much of their mother's money
She visits every Friday but he handles every actual crisis at two in the morning
She refuses to help with medication
quiz.explanation: Bayu complains that despite her regular Friday visits, he is the one handling every real crisis late at night.

quiz.question: What does Bayu accuse Salma of regarding family gatherings?
options: Mentioning her caregiving often enough that it surfaces frequently in conversation
Refusing to discuss their mother's health
quiz.explanation: Bayu points out that her caregiving comes up often enough at gatherings to make him question her motives.

quiz.question: What surprising admission does Bayu make about himself?
options: That he never actually helps their mother
That he wants to stop helping entirely
That he lied about the crises
That some part of him also wants credit for his invisible effort, which unsettles him
quiz.explanation: Bayu admits that despite preferring invisibility in principle, he resents not getting credit, which troubles him more than exhaustion does.

quiz.question: What question does Bayu propose is the real one to ask?
options: Whether either of them can keep showing up once the audience, real or imagined, disappears
quiz.explanation: Bayu suggests the real question is whether they'd continue their devotion without any audience at all.

quiz.question: What do Bayu and Salma agree to at the end?
options: To stop mentioning their caregiving at gatherings and share responsibilities more, including late-night calls
To never speak of the disagreement again
quiz.explanation: They agree to stop mentioning it publicly, and Salma asks Bayu to call her during late-night crises so she can share that burden too.

quiz.question: What do Bayu and Salma discover?
options: Both seek recognition in different forms of care.
Neither has cared for their mother.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports this interpretation of its central argument.

quiz.question: Why is Bayu's criticism not a simple accusation?
options: He wants Salma to stop medication.
He admits resenting the invisibility of his own effort.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports this interpretation of its central argument.

quiz.question: What does their agreement avoid?
options: Using family care as material for reputation.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports this interpretation of its central argument.

quiz.question: How does the ending change the conflict?
options: It replaces rivalry with shared responsibility.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports this interpretation of its central argument.

quiz.question: What question replaces their competition?
options: Whether they will keep serving without an audience.
quiz.explanation: The audio supports this interpretation of its central argument.
